introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et quelques espaces sont manquants à l'impression (question 8 : « between1871and1890 », rétabli en « between 1871 and 1890 ») ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante (dates, traités) ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 4 : l'énoncé imprimé date le déclenchement de la révolte Mau Mau de 1951. L'historiographie situe la montée de la violence en 1950-52 (mouvement interdit en août 1950, état d'urgence proclamé le 20 octobre 1952) ; le sujet est recopié tel quel et le corrigé précise la chronologie sans corriger l'énoncé.

Question 5 : l'Afrique équatoriale française regroupe le Gabon, le Moyen-Congo, l'Oubangui-Chari et le Tchad ; le Cameroun, ancien mandat puis tutelle, n'en faisait pas partie. Les interventions militaires françaises (Gabon 1964, Tchad à partir de la fin des années 1960, Centrafrique 1979) et le rôle du réseau Foccart sont cités selon l'historiographie courante, sans chiffres.

Question 7 : le sujet emploie « romanisation » au sens de la promotion du catholicisme romain par Jacques II ; les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, acquittement des sept évêques et invitation à Guillaume le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre).

Question 9 : le montant des réparations (132 milliards de marks-or, fixé en 1921) et les pertes territoriales sont cités de mémoire historique établie ; aucune statistique de population n'est avancée.

Question 11 : la Banque mondiale et le FMI sont des institutions spécialisées de l'ONU ; l'UNICEF (fonds et non institution spécialisée) n'est volontairement pas traité. Les dates (variole déclarée éradiquée en 1980, Alma-Ata 1978, convention 182 de l'OIT en 1999, Codex Alimentarius 1963, retrait des États-Unis de l'UNESCO en 1984-85) sont citées selon l'historiographie courante.

Question 12 : le sujet vise la rupture sino-soviétique après la mort de Staline (1953). Les dates (discours de Khrouchtchev en février 1956, rupture de l'accord nucléaire en 1959, retrait des conseillers en 1960, congrès de Bucarest en juin 1960, guerre sino-indienne 1962, incidents de l'Oussouri en mars 1969) sont données selon l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre n'est avancé.

Thèmes : les noms sont qualifiés pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone (`sino-soviet split`, `afrikaner nationalism`, `mau mau revolt in kenya`...) ; plusieurs sont réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2021 (`scramble for africa`, `apartheid in south africa`, `cold war`, `indirect rule in colonial africa`) ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the view that the limitations of Christian missionary activities in West Africa outweighed the achievements.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Christian missionary activity in West Africa expanded from the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, when the Church Missionary Society (CMS), the Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society, the Basel Mission, the Bremen Mission and the Church of Scotland mission began work from bases such as Freetown, Cape Coast, Accra, Abeokuta and Calabar. The view in the question is that the weaknesses and damaging side-effects of this work were greater than its benefits. A balanced judgement is that the missionaries' achievements in education, health, language and the ending of some harmful practices were lasting and, on the whole, larger than their limitations, although the limitations were serious and explain the later African reaction against mission control.

**1. Achievements.**
- *Western education.* Missionaries opened the first schools. Fourah Bay College (founded by the CMS in Freetown in 1827) trained teachers, clergy and later professionals; the CMS Grammar School in Freetown (1845) and in Lagos (1859), the Methodist Boys' High School in Lagos (1878) and the Hope Waddell Training Institution at Calabar (1895) produced clerks, teachers, pastors and craftsmen. The mission schools produced most of the first generation of educated Africans, who later became nationalist leaders, journalists and civil servants.
- *Language and literature.* Missionaries reduced many West African languages to writing (Yoruba, Igbo, Efik, Twi, Ewe and others), produced grammars, dictionaries and Bible translations (Samuel Ajayi Crowther was central in Yoruba and Igbo work), and set up printing presses. This preserved vernacular languages and made literacy possible.
- *Health and social welfare.* Mission dispensaries, hospitals and leprosy centres introduced modern medicine and nursing; missionaries also took in freed captives, orphans and the rejected, such as the mothers and the twins in the south-east of Nigeria whom Mary Slessor protected.
- *Humanitarian reform.* They campaigned against the slave trade, human sacrifice, the killing of twins and some ordeals, and promoted "legitimate commerce" and new crops and skills through technical and agricultural training.
- *African leadership in the Church.* Crowther was consecrated the first African Anglican bishop in 1864, which showed that Africans could lead; the idea of a self-governing African church was supported by Henry Venn of the CMS.

**2. Limitations.**
- *Cultural intolerance.* Many missionaries condemned African religion, polygamy, dances, secret societies and ancestor rites as pagan and demanded that converts break from them. This split families and communities and often produced shallow, partly nominal Christianity.
- *Links with colonial expansion.* Missionaries often prepared the ground for European rule, acting as interpreters, consuls' informants and treaty-makers; the saying that the missionary came first, then the trader, then the soldier expresses a criticism of the time. Their schools also taught obedience to colonial rule.
- *Racial attitudes and paternalism.* In the 1880s and 1890s younger European missionaries criticised Crowther's Niger Mission and removed African clergy from senior positions, which was one reason why African members left to form independent churches such as the United Native African Church in Lagos (1891) and, in Cameroon, the Native Baptist Church (1888) after the English Baptist mission in Cameroon was handed over to German missionaries.
- *Rivalry between denominations.* Competition between Catholics, Anglicans, Methodists and Presbyterians divided communities and wasted resources.
- *Limited and unbalanced education.* The schools stressed literary, religious and clerical training rather than technical and industrial training, were concentrated in coastal and southern areas, and produced a small elite that was often cut off from its own society; the Muslim north was deliberately left largely closed to the missions.
- *Material difficulties.* Mission work was limited by shortage of funds and staff and by disease (the Niger Expedition of 1841 lost many of its Europeans to fever), and conversion remained a minority achievement in many areas for several decades.

**3. Evaluation.** The limitations were real but were mostly the faults of the age and of the methods used, whereas the achievements had a permanent effect on the societies of West Africa. Education alone created the leaders who later claimed independence, and the written vernacular languages and mission hospitals are still used today. By contrast, the limitations mostly produced a reaction (African independent churches, cultural nationalism) which itself shaped modern African Christianity.

**Conclusion.** The view that the limitations outweighed the achievements is not convincing. To a large extent the achievements, above all in education, language, health and humanitarian reform, were greater and more durable than the limitations, although the missionaries' cultural intolerance, paternalism and association with colonial conquest sharply reduced their moral authority and sometimes harmed the societies that they served.
themes: christian missionary activity in west africa
